readingPassages.titleEn: Trust in Human Relationships and Warning Signs of Dishonesty
readingPassages.titleAr: الثقة في العلاقات الإنسانية وعلامات التحذير من الخداع
paragraphs: Trust is one of the most valuable things in our lives, yet it's not always easy to know whom we can rely on. While many people act with honesty, others hide their true intentions behind a friendly smile.

In life, not everyone we meet is truly honest. Some people put on a friendly face, but are in fact 'wolves in sheep's clothing.' They may deceive us to gain money, favors, or private information. This can happen anywhere - at school, in the workplace, or even among people we consider friends. For example, someone might act supportively just to borrow money, with no intention of returning it. Another might spread false stories to damage someone's reputation.

This type of dishonesty is not limited to face-to-face interactions. In the digital world, online scammers use deceit to trick innocent people. They make grand promises - such as free prizes, dream jobs, or fast profits - only to exploit our personal data or disappear with our money. It is like being caught in a trap you did not realize was set.

Whether in daily life or online, there are warning signs: The person or platform applies pressure to make you act quickly; the story changes when you ask for details; or the promises seem too good to be true. To protect yourself, pause before acting, ask careful questions, and confirm the facts from reliable sources. As the old saying goes: 'Trust, but verify.' Although dishonesty exists, it should never stop us from believing in the goodness of people. By being cautious, wise, and aware of warning signs, we can protect ourselves and still enjoy healthy, trustworthy relationships.

readingPassages.titleEn: Life Talks: Interview with Dr. Sarah Al-Haddad on Manipulation and Subtle Coercion
readingPassages.titleAr: حديث الحياة: مقابلة مع د. سارة الحداد حول التلاعب والضغط النفسي
paragraphs: Host: Welcome back to 'Life Talks.' Today, we're joined by Dr. Sarah Al-Haddad, a social psychologist who has been studying how people - young and old - can be tricked or pressured into doing things they don't want to do. Welcome, Dr. Sarah.
Dr. Sarah: Thank you. It's an important topic. People often think of scams or theft, but it can also be subtle - like being pushed to work for free, share personal secrets, or support harmful ideas.
Host: So it's not just about money?

Dr. Sarah: Not at all. For teenagers, the pressure might come from friends who want them to join in risky behavior so they can 'fit in.' For older people, it might be someone pretending to help with paperwork, but really trying to take control of their property.
Host: That sounds worrying. How can people avoid such traps?

Dr. Sarah: First, notice your feelings. If you feel rushed, guilty, or afraid, stop and ask yourself, 'Why am I feeling this way?' People who exploit others often use emotional pressure. Second, get a second opinion. Talk to a friend, family member, or trusted advisor before agreeing to anything important. And third, learn to say 'no' without apology. You don't owe an explanation to someone who is trying to use you.
Host: That's great advice. Do you have a final message for our listeners?
Dr. Sarah: Yes: Your time, energy, and trust are valuable. Guard them carefully. If something feels wrong, it probably is.

readingPassages.titleEn: The War of the New Generation: Information Attacks and Cyber Rumors
readingPassages.titleAr: حرب الجيل الجديد: الهجمات المعلوماتية والشائعات الإلكترونية
paragraphs: In the past, wars were fought with soldiers, tanks, and planes. Today, a new kind of war is spreading across the world. It does not use bullets or bombs. Instead, it uses words - lies, half-truths, and rumors. Experts call this the 'war of the new generation.'

In this kind of war, the goal is not to destroy buildings, but to damage trust. Lies can be used to make people angry, afraid, or confused. A rumor can spread quickly through social media, making millions believe something that is not true. When people no longer know what to believe, it becomes easier to control them. The victims of these 'information attacks' can be individuals, communities, or even entire nations.

readingPassages.titleEn: Appearances and Authenticity in Modern Digital Life
readingPassages.titleAr: المظاهر والأصالة في الحياة الرقمية الحديثة
paragraphs: In modern life, appearances can sometimes be misleading, but they also remind us of the importance of being genuine. Social media and advertisements may show perfect images, yet they give us the chance to reflect on what really matters. Instead of comparing ourselves with edited pictures or staged lifestyles, we can use them as motivation to appreciate honesty and real achievements.

Throughout history, people have enjoyed expressing themselves through clothes, art, and language. This creativity can be fun and inspiring, as long as we remember that true worth does not depend on looks alone. Combining external beauty with internal authenticity creates lasting respect.

questions.stemEn: What ______ you do if you won the lottery?
questions.explanationEn: Second conditional question structure: 'What would + subject + do + if + past simple?'.
questions.stem: What ______ you do if you won the lottery?

questions.stemEn: If it rains tomorrow, we ______ the picnic.
questions.explanationEn: First conditional rule: 'If + present simple (rains), subject + will + infinitive (will cancel)'.
questions.stem: If it rains tomorrow, we ______ the picnic.

questions.stemEn: They would travel if they ______ free time.
questions.explanationEn: Second conditional clause: 'would travel if + past simple (had)'.
questions.stem: They would travel if they ______ free time.

questions.stemEn: If you mix red and blue, you ______ purple.
questions.explanationEn: Zero conditional for general scientific facts: 'If + present simple, present simple (get)'.
questions.stem: If you mix red and blue, you ______ purple.

questions.stemEn: If I ______ enough money for the project, I wouldn't have to borrow from the bank.
questions.explanationEn: Second conditional: 'If + past simple (had), wouldn't have to borrow'. Expresses an unreal present situation.
questions.stem: If I ______ enough money for the project, I wouldn't have to borrow from the bank.

questions.stemEn: If he paid more attention in class, he wouldn't misunderstand the lesson. This means that he ______ enough attention in class.
questions.explanationEn: The second conditional describes an imaginary or contrary-to-fact situation in the present. Therefore, 'If he paid...' means he currently 'doesn't pay' attention.
questions.stem: If he paid more attention in class, he wouldn't misunderstand the lesson. This means that he ______ enough attention in class.

questions.stemEn: If I were you, I ______ the homework.
questions.explanationEn: 'If I were you, I would...' is the standard structure used for giving advice in English.
questions.stem: If I were you, I ______ the homework.

questions.stemEn: If I ______ help with a school project, I look online.
questions.explanationEn: Zero conditional used for habitual personal routines: 'If + present simple (need), present simple (look)'.
questions.stem: If I ______ help with a school project, I look online.

questions.stemEn: Call the ambulance ______ emergency.
questions.explanationEn: 'In case of' is followed by a noun phrase ('in case of emergency'), whereas 'if' requires a full clause.
questions.stem: Call the ambulance ______ emergency.

questions.stemEn: ______ training is useful for you, you should do it every day.
questions.explanationEn: 'If' introduces the conditional condition followed by subject + verb ('training is useful').
questions.stem: ______ training is useful for you, you should do it every day.

questions.stemEn: ______ you have any problem, give me a ring immediately.
questions.explanationEn: Inversion of If: 'Should you have...' replaces 'If you have...' in conditional structures.
questions.stem: ______ you have any problem, give me a ring immediately.

questions.stemEn: When I spend much time on computer, I always ______ a severe headache.
questions.explanationEn: 'When / If + present simple, present simple' expresses a repeated personal fact or natural consequence.
questions.stem: When I spend much time on computer, I always ______ a severe headache.

questions.stemEn: If you heat water to 100°C, it ______.
questions.explanationEn: Scientific fact taking zero conditional: 'If + present simple, present simple (it evaporates)'.
questions.stem: If you heat water to 100°C, it ______.

questions.stemEn: Amira wouldn't have been a doctor, ______ studying hard hadn't been an important thing.
questions.explanationEn: Third conditional clause: 'Amira wouldn't have been a doctor if studying hard hadn't been an important thing'.
questions.stem: Amira wouldn't have been a doctor, ______ studying hard hadn't been an important thing.

questions.stemEn: ______ his injury, he could participate in the competition.
questions.explanationEn: 'But for' means 'without' or 'if it were not for', and is followed by a noun phrase ('his injury').
questions.stem: ______ his injury, he could participate in the competition.

questions.stemEn: ______ working hard is one of your traits (صفات), it will be hard to succeed in life.
questions.explanationEn: 'Unless' means 'if not'. Unless working hard is one of your traits = If working hard is not one of your traits.
questions.stem: ______ working hard is one of your traits (صفات), it will be hard to succeed in life.

questions.stemEn: If you press this button, this machine ______.
questions.explanationEn: Mechanical instruction / zero conditional: 'If you press, it operates'.
questions.stem: If you press this button, this machine ______.

questions.stemEn: She would have won that medal if she ______ well.
questions.explanationEn: Third conditional formula: 'would have + pp if + past perfect (had played)'.
questions.stem: She would have won that medal if she ______ well.
